column3: A ruling people reject believing two human messengers because their people are subject to them, directly exposing status and domination as false measures of truth.
Its general statement that God's remainder is better for believers does not clarify the contempt for Noah's followers.
It contrasts those who believe with those who turn away, but adds no social-rank dimension to the focus objection.
Noah's chiefs explicitly dismiss his followers as their lowliest, making this the closest narrative and verbal parallel.
Noah refuses to claim knowledge of the followers' deeds, beginning his answer to the status-based objection.
It defines a broad faith-and-righteousness criterion without addressing who is deemed worthy to belong.
A believer within Pharaoh's household invites his people to follow him to right guidance, contrasting elite resistance with a call grounded in guidance.
Noah explicitly refuses to drive away the believers, directly overturning the exclusion demanded by the focus speakers.
The messenger is commanded to remain with devoted worshippers and not seek worldly adornment, directly countering elite preference over faithful companions.
It presents believers who follow the Prophet as part of the supported community, giving positive weight to the group the focus speakers disparage.
A believing man defends a messenger before Pharaoh's establishment despite its hostility, showing truth contested within a dominant social order.
Its contrast between following God's pleasure and incurring wrath is a general alternative to the focus rejection.
Rejecters call believers fools, and the verse reverses that judgment, directly paralleling contemptuous refusal to believe with a despised group.
Noah assigns the followers' account to his Lord, completing his reply that social observers cannot judge their standing.
The statement that few believe addresses disbelief generally, not contempt for believers' social position.
Following Satan rather than remaining among God's servants is a broad contrary use of following.
It defines closeness to Abraham by following him and believing, but does not address social disparagement.
Moses' request to follow a teacher for learning does not materially clarify the focus scene.
Hud's people reject belief and refuse to abandon their gods, supplying a related pattern of prophetic refusal but not the low-status rationale.
Noah identifies himself as a clear warner, clarifying the prophetic role that his opponents dismiss through their followers.
The warning that God's punishment is not secure does not add to the focus objection.
Pharaoh's people promise belief under affliction, a limited contrast with their earlier refusal.
Abraham's identity as a devoted monotheist offers no specific clarification of judging followers by rank.
Provision and security in Quraysh do not materially illuminate the focus scene.
The brothers' request for their father's trust uses a different sense of security and faith.
The opponents escalate from rejection to threatening Noah, showing the coercive consequence of the preceding exclusionary objection.
Following victorious magicians is a conditional allegiance to apparent power, only indirectly related to the focus speakers' status criterion.
Disbelievers urge believers to follow their path while falsely offering to bear the cost, exposing pressure on faith-based allegiance.
It identifies failure to believe in God as a final condemnation, without the social mechanism of the focus refusal.
The rhetorical question about what message they will believe after this marks persistent disbelief generally.
The phrase about decrepit old age is unrelated to the focus's contemptuous label for followers.
Noah and those with him are saved in the laden ship, giving the narrative outcome for the community the opponents scorned.
The challenge to produce a more guiding book concerns evidentiary comparison rather than the worth of followers.
The request for a barrier against Gog and Magog does not clarify the focus objection.
Noah rejects claims to angelic privilege and denies that those despised by his opponents will receive no good from God, directly answering the same social contempt.
A coerced claim of belief during punishment is only a distant contrast to the refusal in the focus.
The resurrection proof and its mention of old age do not materially address the focus scene.
The passage on trust and dishonesty toward others does not clarify contempt for Noah's followers.
The question about following Aaron concerns obedience within Moses' community, not social rank as a basis for disbelief.
Another people dismiss their messenger as bewitched, supplying a same-surah pattern of discrediting a prophetic caller.
Shu'ayb's call to worship God and trade justly is a general prophetic parallel without the focus's status objection.
It depicts persecution of believers, but does not explain the social judgment voiced in the focus.
The demand for a material miracle makes belief conditional on the opponents' preferred terms, paralleling refusal to receive the messenger on proper grounds.
Believers are told to think well of one another, offering only a broad social ethic against disparagement.
Following a course in Dhul-Qarnayn's travels does not clarify the focus.
The repeated charge that a messenger is bewitched reinforces the same-surah pattern of dismissing prophetic speech rather than considering it.
The account of slander and its consequences does not materially clarify the focus objection.
Creation as a sign for believers adds no distinct insight into judging Noah's followers.
The idolaters briefly acknowledge their own wrongdoing, a distant contrast to the focus speakers' unexamined judgment.
Etiquette before God and the Messenger does not directly address the focus scene.
Shu'ayb's ethical and monotheistic call does not add to the social-status objection already covered.
Pharaoh's people pre-classify every sign as magic and refuse belief, illustrating a settled rejection that evidence does not move.
Belief mixed with association is a general qualification of faith, not a clarification of despised followers.
Calling the recipient of revelation mad is another form of dismissing a messenger rather than hearing his call.
The instruction not to question a teacher prematurely does not clarify the focus.
The prohibition of despair after good news does not bear on the focus objection.
God's varying provision as a sign for believers does not materially explain the focus scene.
The demand to see God openly before believing shows belief made conditional on opponents' terms, a related refusal pattern.
The trusted angel's obedience does not clarify the social status of believers.
Hud's chiefs call him foolish and a liar, showing elites discrediting a prophet through contempt rather than engagement.
It imagines people wishing they had followed God's signs before humiliation, contrasting the focus speakers' present refusal with its foreseeable regret.
Pharaoh's chiefs frame Moses and his people as a threat to their order and answer with coercion, closely related to elite resistance toward a believing group.
The reward for believers who do good does not add to the focus's social objection.
The prayer for a submitting community offers a broad positive image of collective faith.
Aaron tells his people to follow him and obey his command instead of the calf, setting guided communal allegiance against a false social current.
It assigns disbelief to those who refused faith, but does not clarify why the focus speakers demean believers.
A sign for believers in the ruins does not materially develop the focus scene.
The disciples join belief in revelation with following the messenger, directly supplying the positive allegiance the focus speakers reject.
The high ranks promised to believing righteous people modestly reverse the focus speakers' assumption that believers are lowly.
Abraham's model of dissociation from idolatry is a general contrast to communal unbelief.
Noah's designation as a believing servant affirms his faith but adds little beyond the same narrative already present.
The question to Iblis about failing to prostrate does not clarify the focus objection.
Following the recitation concerns the reception of revelation, not the social standing of followers.
The raising of the Prophet's mention does not materially illuminate the focus scene.
The preference for kind speech over hurtful charity gives a limited ethical counterpoint to contemptuous social speech.
The expansion of the Prophet's breast does not clarify the focus objection.
Abraham's designation as a believing servant is only a generic faith parallel.
Iblis is expelled and made among the lowly because of arrogance, sharply reversing the hierarchy assumed by the focus speakers.
Joseph's rejection of a faithless people's way is a broad contrast with unbelieving communal norms.
The accusation that the revelation was fabricated is presented as a result of their unbelief, another way rejection manufactures a pretext.
The description of Moses and Aaron as believing servants offers only a generic parallel.
The disputing idolaters in Hell belong to a later same-surah judgment scene, but it does not directly clarify Noah's social objection.
Elijah's designation as a believing servant is only a generic faith parallel.
The angels' question about humanity's future corruption is not a contemptuous judgment of believers and only distantly relates to group evaluation.
It calls believers who do righteous deeds the best of creation, directly reversing the focus speakers' verdict that believers are lowest.
The universal command to believe in and follow the messenger provides the positive norm opposed by the focus speakers' refusal.
It forbids one group from mocking another because the mocked may be better, directly condemning the evaluative error behind calling followers lowly.
People refuse to follow guidance for fear of being uprooted from their land, giving a close parallel in which perceived worldly loss blocks allegiance.
The question why people do not believe and spend is a general reproach without the focus's social mechanism.
The distinction between truthful and lying excuse-makers does not clarify the focus scene.
A crowd orders Abraham burned in defense of its gods, showing rejection of a prophetic challenge becoming collective violence.
Pharaoh's magicians endure persecution precisely because they believed God's signs, contrasting faithful response with the rulers' hostility.
The introduction of Noah as a clear warner supplies the immediate narrative frame for the same people's objection in the focus.
Repentance and faith after wrongdoing give a general path away from disbelief, without the social-rank issue.
The angel's announcement of a pure son does not clarify the focus objection.
Moses links Pharaoh and his chiefs' wealth and splendor with leading people astray, explaining how elite advantage can distort response to guidance.
David's recognition of wrongdoing and repentance only broadly contrasts with the focus speakers' error.
It links unalloyed faith to security and guidance, but does not address the status of the believing community.
It distinguishes spoken belief from belief in the heart, a limited contrast to the focus speakers' open refusal.
People given knowledge respond to recitation with prostration, contrasting receptive recognition with rejection based on social judgment.
Noah says he will not drive away believers, who will meet their Lord; it is the clearest direct answer to the exclusion implied by 26:111.
The messenger is forbidden to drive away those who call on their Lord, directly establishing that believers cannot be excluded for others' social judgments.
The elite ask whether these are the people God favored among them, making explicit the same contemptuous status test behind the focus objection.
Noah asks who would protect him from God if he drove the believers away, completing the moral and theological rejection of the demand in 26:111.
The arrogant chiefs question the weak believers' allegiance to Salih, directly staging faith as a conflict between social rank and recognition of God's messenger.
The Israelites object to Talut's authority because he lacks wealth and status, while the verse replaces those criteria with divine election, knowledge, and strength.
Disbelievers ridicule believers, while the God-conscious will be above them at judgment; it directly reverses the focus speakers' social verdict.
Human rank is grounded in God-consciousness rather than lineage or status, supplying the governing criterion that the focus speakers ignore.
The hypocrites plan to expel the humbler from the city in the name of the mightier, closely paralleling exclusionary status politics against believers.
Pharaoh dismisses Moses as insignificant and lacking visible wealth, a direct parallel in which worldly rank is used to reject a messenger.
The chiefs call Noah only a human seeking superiority over them, revealing the same elite suspicion that a prophetic call threatens established rank.
The chiefs warn that obeying a human like themselves would mean loss, directly tying refusal of a messenger to perceived social diminishment.
People reject the guidance because they cannot accept that God sent a human messenger, closely paralleling status-based resistance to prophetic authority.
The wrongdoers privately reduce the messenger to a human like themselves and his message to magic, another direct form of elite dismissal.
Thamud ask whether they should follow one human from among them, making the social unacceptability of following a human messenger explicit.
Messengers acknowledge being human like their peoples but locate their distinction in God's favor, directly answering the recurrent objection to human messengers.
Noah's chiefs call him plainly astray, supplying the earlier narrative form of their contemptuous rejection.
Shu'ayb's people say they see him as weak among them, an especially close parallel in which perceived social weakness is used to dismiss a prophet.
Noah's call to fear God and obey him immediately precedes the focus objection, making the rejected demand itself explicit.
Noah's refusal to seek payment removes an ordinary worldly-interest explanation before the opponents turn to the status of his followers.
Noah names his people's rejection after their threat, preserving the full escalation from social refusal to open hostility.
Noah asks for decisive separation and salvation for himself and the believers with him, giving the outcome sought for the disparaged community.
The drowning of the remaining rejecters completes the same-surah outcome of the conflict introduced at 26:111.
The arrogant explicitly refuse what the weak believers affirm about Salih, completing the class-divided response begun in 7:75.
Noah's people demand he stop arguing and bring the threatened punishment, showing the hardening that follows their refusal.
Noah answers his people's mockery with the prospect of reciprocal exposure, continuing the narrative of contempt toward him and his followers.
Communities object that messengers are only humans like themselves and refuse to abandon inherited worship, combining the two recurring rejection formulas.
The astonishment that a warning came to a human messenger supplies another concise instance of resistance to ordinary human prophethood.
The arrogant declare they will never believe in this Quran, while the later scene exposes the mutual blame of leaders and followers.
The arrogant deny that they barred the weak from guidance, directly naming the social asymmetry between dominant rejecters and those beneath them.
The weak accuse the arrogant of directing their disbelief, supplying a judgment-scene reckoning for hierarchical influence.
Rejecters refuse to feed the needy by invoking God's will, showing a related use of religious language to preserve social indifference.
The chiefs find it strange that a warner came from among them and organize resistance, presenting elite coordination against a messenger.
People tell their messengers that they are only humans like themselves, reiterating the objection to human messengers in a broader prophetic pattern.
A community follows the way of its forefathers under the leadership of its affluent class, identifying inherited elite custom as a barrier to guidance.
The objection that the Quran was not sent to a great man from the two cities directly treats worldly prominence as a qualification for revelation.
The claim that revelation is inherited magic is a related strategy of dismissing the message without receiving its warning.
Criminals laugh at believers, giving a later and explicit instance of social ridicule directed at the faithful.
The final reversal, in which believers laugh at disbelievers, gives the judgment outcome that overturns present mockery.
